disclaimer: These are illustrative, synthetic reference profiles built from the public Child-Pugh cirrhosis staging system and typical liver function reference ranges. They are NOT real patient records and are NOT individually cited the way the drug PK table requires. Treat them as placeholder data to unblock rendering and simulation, and replace with reviewed, cited values before any claim beyond a hackathon demo.

field_notes.child_pugh_class: Child-Pugh class A (mild), B (moderate) or C (severe) cirrhosis severity, or 'none' for a non-cirrhotic liver
field_notes.child_pugh_score: The underlying 5-15 point score (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy) that the class is derived from
field_notes.alt_u_l: Alanine aminotransferase, a liver-cell-injury marker; rises with active damage (e.g. fatty liver, acute injury)
field_notes.ast_u_l: Aspartate aminotransferase, a second liver-cell-injury marker
field_notes.total_bilirubin_mg_dl: Bilirubin level; rises as the liver's ability to process and excrete it falls
field_notes.albumin_g_dl: Protein the liver synthesizes; falls as synthetic function declines
field_notes.inr: International normalized ratio for blood clotting; rises as the liver's clotting-factor production declines
field_notes.hepatic_blood_flow_multiplier: Relative effective blood flow through functioning liver tissue (1.0 = normal); portal hypertension and shunting reduce this
field_notes.cyp450_activity_multiplier: Relative drug-metabolizing enzyme activity (1.0 = normal); falls as liver cells are lost or damaged, slowing metabolism of most drugs
field_notes.first_pass_bioavailability_multiplier: Relative multiplier on how much of an oral dose reaches the bloodstream unchanged (1.0 = normal); cirrhosis increases this because portal blood bypasses the liver through shunts, so MORE drug escapes first-pass metabolism
field_notes.clearance_scaling_factor: Relative multiplier applied to a hepatically-cleared drug's normal clearance rate (1.0 = healthy baseline, lower = drug stays in the body longer)
field_notes.hepatotoxic_sensitivity_multiplier: Relative multiplier for how much a hepatotoxic drug (e.g. paracetamol overdose, some antibiotics) damages this liver per unit exposure (1.0 = healthy baseline)

profiles.label: Healthy adult liver
profiles.basis: Standard healthy-adult reference ranges for ALT, AST, bilirubin, albumin and INR

profiles.label: Early non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), no fibrosis
profiles.basis: Early fatty liver typically shows mildly elevated ALT/AST with still-normal synthetic function (albumin, INR); clotting and protein levels are unaffected before fibrosis develops

profiles.label: Compensated cirrhosis, Child-Pugh A (alcohol-related)
profiles.basis: Child-Pugh A is 5-6 points; this profile uses mildly abnormal bilirubin, albumin and INR consistent with that score, with no ascites or encephalopathy

profiles.label: Cirrhosis, Child-Pugh B (chronic viral hepatitis)
profiles.basis: Child-Pugh B is 7-9 points; this profile assumes mild ascites controlled with medication, with moderately abnormal bilirubin, albumin and INR

profiles.label: Decompensated cirrhosis, Child-Pugh C
profiles.basis: Child-Pugh C is 10-15 points; ALT/AST can actually look lower than Child-Pugh B here because so little functioning liver tissue remains to release enzymes, while bilirubin, albumin and INR are severely abnormal and ascites/encephalopathy are typically present

profiles.label: Recovering from acute drug-induced liver injury (e.g. paracetamol overdose)
profiles.basis: Acute injury shows very high ALT/AST (cell death in progress) with albumin still near-normal because synthetic function has not had time to fall as far as in chronic cirrhosis; INR is elevated because clotting-factor production is acutely impaired; this profile exists to demo acute vs. chronic patterns looking different even at similar overall severity
